nodes.title: Electrolytes & Degree of Dissociation
points: Strong Electrolytes: Dissociate completely in aqueous solution (α ≈ 1). Examples: Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄), Strong bases (NaOH, KOH), Salts (NaCl, KCl).

Weak Electrolytes: Dissociate only to a small extent in aqueous solution (α ≪ 1). Dynamic equilibrium exists between ions and unionized molecules. Examples: Weak acids (CH₃COOH, HCN, HCOOH), Weak bases (NH₄OH, amines).
Degree of Dissociation (α): Fraction of total moles of electrolyte that dissociates into ions: α = (Moles dissociated) / (Total moles). Percent dissociation = α × 100%.

nodes.title: Acid-Base Theories & Conjugate Pairs
points: Arrhenius Theory: Acid produces H⁺ (H₃O⁺) in water; Base produces OH⁻ in water. Limitation: Applies only to aqueous solutions.
Brønsted-Lowry Theory: Acid is a proton (H⁺) DONOR; Base is a proton (H⁺) ACCEPTOR.
Conjugate Acid-Base Pair: A pair of substances that differ by only a single proton (H⁺).
Acid ⇌ Conjugate Base + H⁺; Base + H⁺ ⇌ Conjugate Acid. (Strong acid has weak conjugate base; weak acid has strong conjugate base).
Amphoteric Nature of Water: Water acts as acid with NH₃ and as base with HCl.
Lewis Theory: Acid is an electron-pair ACCEPTOR (electrophiles: BF₃, AlCl₃, H⁺, metal cations); Base is an electron-pair DONOR (nucleophiles: NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻, halide ions).

nodes.title: Ostwald's Dilution Law
points: Applies to WEAK electrolytes only.
For Weak Acid (HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻): K_a = (α² C) / (1 − α). Since α ≪ 1, (1 − α) ≈ 1 ⟹ K_a = α² C ⟹ α = √(K_a / C) = √(K_a · V).
Hydrogen ion concentration: [H⁺] = α C = √(K_a · C).
For Weak Base (BOH ⇌ B⁺ + OH⁻): K_b = α² C ⟹ α = √(K_b / C) = √(K_b · V).
Hydroxide ion concentration: [OH⁻] = α C = √(K_b · C).
Ostwald's Principle: Degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte is inversely proportional to square root of concentration (directly proportional to square root of dilution).

nodes.title: Autoionization of Water & pH Scale
points: Autoionization (Self-ionization) of Water: H₂O + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
Ionic Product of Water (K_w): K_w = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K (25 °C).
In pure neutral water at 298 K: [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ M.
pH and pOH Definitions:
pH = −log₁₀[H₃O⁺]; pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻].
Fundamental Identity: pH + pOH = pK_w = 14 at 298 K.
Temperature Dependence: Autoionization is endothermic. As temperature increases, K_w increases, so pH of pure neutral water becomes < 7 (though water remains neutral as [H⁺] = [OH⁻]).

nodes.title: Hydrolysis of Salts & Solution pH
points: Salt Hydrolysis: Interaction of ions of a salt with water to produce acidity or alkalinity.
1. Strong Acid + Strong Base (NaCl, KNO₃): Neither ion hydrolyzes. Neutral solution: pH = 7.
2. Strong Acid + Weak Base (NH₄Cl, CuSO₄): Cation hydrolyzes (Cationic hydrolysis). Acidic solution: pH = 7 − ½ pK_b − ½ log₁₀C < 7.
3. Weak Acid + Strong Base (CH₃COONa, NaCN): Anion hydrolyzes (Anionic hydrolysis). Basic solution: pH = 7 + ½ pK_a + ½ log₁₀C > 7.
4. Weak Acid + Weak Base (CH₃COONH₄, NH₄CN): Both cation and anion hydrolyze. pH = 7 + ½ pK_a − ½ pK_b.
CRITICAL: pH of weak acid + weak base salt is completely INDEPENDENT of concentration C!

formulas.label: Weak acid + Weak base pH
formulas.expr: pH = 7 + ½ pK_a − ½ pK_b (independent of C)

nodes.title: Buffer Solutions & Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation
points: Buffer Solution: A solution that resists drastic changes in pH upon addition of small amounts of strong acid, strong base, or on dilution.
Acidic Buffer: Weak acid + its salt with strong base (e.g., CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa).
Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation (Acidic): pH = pK_a + log₁₀([Salt] / [Acid]).
Basic Buffer: Weak base + its salt with strong acid (e.g., NH₄OH + NH₄Cl).
Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation (Basic): pOH = pK_b + log₁₀([Salt] / [Base]), and pH = 14 − pOH.
Buffer Capacity: Maximum when [Salt] = [Acid] ⟹ pH = pK_a.
Buffer Range: pH = pK_a ± 1.

nodes.title: Solubility Product (K_sp) & Precipitation
points: For a sparingly soluble salt A_x B_y(s) ⇌ x A^(y+) + y B^(x−):
Solubility Product: K_sp = [A^(y+)]^x [B^(x−)]^y = x^x y^y S^(x + y), where S is molar solubility.
Solubility Product Expressions:
1. 1:1 Salt (AgCl, BaSO₄): K_sp = S² ⟹ S = √K_sp.
2. 1:2 or 2:1 Salt (PbCl₂, CaF₂, Ag₂CrO₄): K_sp = (1)¹(2)² S³ = 4S³ ⟹ S = (K_sp / 4)^(1/3).
3. 1:3 Salt (Al(OH)₃, Fe(OH)₃): K_sp = (1)¹(3)³ S⁴ = 27S⁴ ⟹ S = (K_sp / 27)^(1/4).
Condition for Precipitation (Ionic Product IP vs K_sp):
1. IP < K_sp: Unsaturated solution (no precipitate, more solute dissolves).
2. IP = K_sp: Saturated solution (dynamic equilibrium).
3. IP > K_sp: Supersaturated solution ⟹ PRECIPITATION OCCURS.

nodes.title: Common Ion Effect & Applications
points: Common Ion Effect: The suppression of the degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte by the addition of a strong electrolyte having an ion in common.
Example: Dissociation of weak CH₃COOH is suppressed by adding strong CH₃COONa (equilibrium shifts left per Le Chatelier's principle).
Applications in Qualitative Salt Analysis:
1. Group II Cations (Cu²⁺, Pb²⁺): Precipitated as sulfides using H₂S in presence of dil. HCl. Common ion H⁺ suppresses H₂S dissociation, lowering [S²⁻] so only low K_sp Group II sulfides precipitate.

2. Group III Cations (Fe³⁺, Al³⁺): Precipitated as hydroxides using NH₄OH in presence of NH₄Cl. Common ion NH₄⁺ suppresses NH₄OH dissociation, ensuring only low K_sp Group III hydroxides precipitate without precipitating Group IV/V cations.
3. Purification of NaCl: Passing HCl gas through saturated brine precipitates pure NaCl as common ion Cl⁻ exceeds K_sp.

formulas.label: Common ion equilibrium shift
formulas.expr: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (Adding CH₃COONa shifts left)

formulas.label: Group II precipitation
formulas.expr: H₂S in dil. HCl ⟶ Lower [S²⁻] precipitates only Group II

nodes.title: Must-Know Board Derivations & Proofs
points: Board Favourite #1: Derive Ostwald's dilution law for a weak acid (K_a = α² C) and show that α = √(K_a / C).
Board Favourite #2: Derive relationship between pH and pOH: pH + pOH = 14 at 298 K.
Board Favourite #3: Derive Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer solution.
Board Favourite #4: Derive relationship between molar solubility (S) and solubility product (K_sp) for: (1) 1:1 salt, (2) 1:2 salt.
Board Favourite #5: Define: (1) Common ion effect, (2) Buffer solution, (3) Hydrolysis of salt, (4) Solubility product.

nodes.title: MHT-CET Shortcuts, Dilution Traps & Qualitative Tricks
points: Dilute Acid pH Trap: pH of 10⁻⁸ M HCl is NOT 8 (an acid cannot have basic pH!). Account for water autoionization: [H⁺] = 10⁻⁸ + 10⁻⁷ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁷ M ⟹ pH ≈ 6.96.
Dilute Base pH Trap: pH of 10⁻⁸ M NaOH is ≈ 7.04 (slightly basic).
Weak Acid + Weak Base Salt Shortcut: pH = 7 + ½ pK_a − ½ pK_b. If pK_a = pK_b (like CH₃COONH₄), pH = 7.0 (neutral), independent of concentration!
Solubility in Presence of Common Ion: Solubility of AgCl in C molar NaCl: S' = K_sp / C (drastically reduced compared to √K_sp in pure water).
Buffer Capacity Rule: Buffer capacity is maximum when [Salt] = [Acid] (or [Base]), at which point pH = pK_a.
